# Public Star Driving School: full site content

Source: https://publicstardrivingschool.com/ . Generated 2026-11-20. Prices are in Canadian dollars; HST is 13%.

Public Star Driving School is an MTO-approved driving school in Ajax, Ontario, Canada, offering one-on-one G2 and G driving lessons, road test packages and the Beginner Driver Education (BDE) course with free pick-up and drop-off in Scarborough, North York, Pickering, Ajax, Whitby and Oshawa. G2 lessons start at $50/hour + HST ($56.50) and G lessons at $60/hour + HST ($67.80).

- Business name: Public Star Driving School
- Type: Driving school (MTO-approved Beginner Driver Education provider)

- Phone (call or text): (437) 777-4494

- Nearby DriveTest centres we train for: Metro East (Scarborough), Port Union (Scarborough), Downsview (North York), Oshawa
- Lessons: one-on-one, in dual-brake insured cars, free pick-up and drop-off at home, school or work
- Road test packages include use of the instructor's car and a warm-up lesson
- Help booking DriveTest road test appointments
- Lessons available in more than one language; ask when booking
- No payment needed to request a booking

## Frequently asked questions

Q: Do I need to complete the full BDE course to take lessons?
A: No. If you already have a G1 or G2, you can book individual lessons or an hours-plus-road-test bundle without enrolling in the full course.

Q: What does the BDE certificate get me?
A: Graduating from a Ministry-approved BDE course lets you take your G2 road test after 8 months instead of 12, and most insurers offer a discount for new drivers who complete it.

Q: Can I use your car for my road test?
A: Yes. Every hours-plus-road-test bundle and the Premium and Advanced BDE packages include the use of the instructor's car on test day, along with a warm-up lesson beforehand.

Q: How do pick-up and drop-off work?
A: Your instructor picks you up from your home, school or workplace within our service area and drops you off at the end of the lesson, at no extra charge.

Q: How do I pay?
A: No payment is required to request a booking. We'll confirm your schedule first and arrange payment by e-transfer or in person before your first lesson.

Q: Can I book my DriveTest appointment through you?
A: Yes. We'll help you find and book an available road test slot at the DriveTest centre closest to you.

# What to Bring to Your Road Test in Ontario: A Day-Of Checklist

URL: https://publicstardrivingschool.com/blog/what-to-bring-to-road-test-ontario/
Published: 2026-11-20. Updated: 2026-11-20.

Quick answer: For an Ontario G2 or G road test, DriveTest says to bring your current driver's licence, a vehicle in good working order with enough gas, glasses or contacts if you need them to drive, and a printout of your road test confirmation email. Arrive at least 30 minutes early. The road test fee ($53.75 for G2, $91.25 for G) is prepaid when you book, so you only need money on the day if you are hoping for a standby appointment.

Road test day is stressful enough without realizing in the parking lot that your licence is at home or the car has a burnt-out brake light. The good news is that the list of things to bring is short. This guide covers exactly what DriveTest asks for, what to check on the car, how the day runs, and the small extras that make it easier.

## What does DriveTest say to bring to a road test?

DriveTest's road test page lists six things to bring on test day:

1. A vehicle in good working order. DriveTest does not provide cars.
2. Glasses or contact lenses, if you need them to drive.
3. Enough gas in the vehicle to take the test.
4. Your current driver's licence.
5. A printout of your road test confirmation email.
6. Money for test fees, only if you are hoping for a standby road test appointment.

That is the whole official list. Everything else in this guide is about making sure each item is ready.

## Your licence and confirmation email

Bring the driver's licence you are testing on: your G1 if you are taking the G2 test, or your G2 if you are taking the G test. Check the expiry date the week before. DriveTest says novice drivers may not book a road test after their licence expiry date, and you can only keep taking tests while your licence is valid.

Print the confirmation email you got when you booked, since DriveTest lists it as an item to bring.

## Glasses or contact lenses

If you need corrective lenses to drive, wear them for the test. If you wear contacts, a spare pair of glasses is a smart backup.

## What the car needs on test day

You must bring a Class G vehicle of the right class to the centre. DriveTest says it can be owned, borrowed or rented, and it does not need to be a driving instructor's vehicle. Low-speed vehicles cannot be used.

Before the test starts, the examiner walks around the car looking for damage, safety hazards and anything that would stop the test. If the car does not meet the minimum standards, the test can be declared "out of order" and you lose 50% of your prepaid road test fee.

Check these the day before, with a helper standing outside the car:

| Check | What to look for |
| --- | --- |
| Lights | Headlights, brake lights and all four turn signals work |
| Horn and brakes | Horn sounds, brakes and parking brake work |
| Windshield and mirrors | No crack in your line of sight, mirrors intact |
| Seatbelts | Both front belts buckle and release |
| Dashboard | No warning lights suggesting the car is unsafe |
| Fuel | Enough gas to finish the whole test without stopping |
| Documents | Ownership and proof of insurance in the car |

Our guide to G2 road test automatic fails (/blog/g2-road-test-automatic-fails/) explains the car problems that end a test before it starts, and renting a car for your road test (/blog/road-test-car-rental-ontario/) covers your options if your own car is not ready.

### Turn off cameras and recording devices

DriveTest does not allow in-vehicle recording devices during road tests, including cell phones, dashboard cameras and action cameras. They must be disabled. If the car has a camera that cannot be turned off, you must confirm out loud that it is not recording the passenger compartment or pointed at the examiner. If you cannot confirm that, the test is declared out of order.

Put your phone on silent and out of reach before the examiner gets in.

## Who can come with you

No pets and no passengers other than the examiner are allowed in the car during the test. Friends, family and your driving instructor can wait in the designated safe areas. DriveTest says you can, with consent, use a translator or driving instructor during check-in and at the debrief after the test.

Plan your trip there and back:

- Taking the G2 test on a G1? G1 rules mean you must always drive with a fully licensed driver who has at least four years of driving experience, so you cannot drive yourself to or from the centre alone.
- Taking the G test on a G2? DriveTest suggests making plans for getting home if you are not successful, either an accompanying driver or other transportation.

With a driving school road test package, our instructor brings the car and handles the trip, so this part is taken care of.

## How the day runs

1. Arrive at least 30 minutes early. DriveTest asks for this, and arriving late means losing your prepaid fee.
2. Park and check in inside. Most centres have a self-serve kiosk; see a customer service agent if yours does not.
3. Go back to the car and wait. The examiner comes to you. If no one arrives within 30 minutes of your appointment time, go back inside to Counter A.
4. Listen to the instructions. The examiner explains the test before you start and is not allowed to coach you, so ask any questions first.
5. Drive the test. The G2 test usually takes about 20 minutes and the G test about 30 minutes.
6. Get your summary. The examiner gives you a short verbal summary. If you pass, go back inside to apply your results and get a temporary licence.

Road tests run in any weather unless you are told otherwise. If the weather looks bad, check DriveTest's Service Disruptions page on the morning of your test.

## What does the road test cost?

These are DriveTest's current fees, which include taxes:

| DriveTest fee | Amount |
| --- | --- |
| Class G2 road test | $53.75 |
| Class G road test | $91.25 |
| Class G1 licence package (knowledge test, G2 road test and five-year licence) | $159.75 |

Road test fees are prepaid when you book, so you do not need to bring money for a regular appointment. If you cancel within 48 hours, arrive late or do not show up, you lose the prepaid fee unless an exception such as illness with proof applies. Fees can change, so confirm them on the DriveTest fee list (https://drivetest.ca/tests/fees/) when you book.

If you want our car for the test, Public Star's G2 packages with a road test start at $200 + HST ($226.00) for 2 hours of lessons plus the test, and our most popular G2 package is 5 hours + road test for $330 + HST ($372.90). G packages with a road test start at $250 + HST ($282.50). These are separate from DriveTest's fee. See our driving lesson cost guide (/blog/driving-lessons-cost-ontario/) for every package.

If nerves are a bigger worry than the checklist, our guide on beating road test anxiety (/blog/road-test-anxiety-tips/) has practical ways to stay calm, and our winter driving tips for new drivers (/blog/winter-driving-tips-new-drivers/) help if your test is in the cold months.

## Taking your road test in Scarborough or Durham Region

We take students to their road tests across Scarborough, North York, Pickering, Ajax, Whitby and Oshawa, including the Port Union (/blog/port-union-drivetest-guide/), Metro East (/blog/metro-east-drivetest-tips/) and Oshawa (/blog/oshawa-drivetest-tips/) DriveTest centres. Every road test package includes a warm-up lesson in the same car you will test in, so your first drive of the day is not the test itself. For the driving part, read how to pass your G2 road test on the first try (/blog/how-to-pass-g2-road-test/).

## Frequently asked questions

### Do I need to bring my booking confirmation to the road test?

DriveTest lists a printout of your road test confirmation email as one of the items to bring. It is a good idea to have it with you at check-in.

### Do I need to pay at the DriveTest centre on test day?

Not for a regular booked test. Road test fees are prepaid when you book. DriveTest only says to bring money for test fees if you are hoping for a standby appointment.

### Can I use my phone or dashcam during the road test?

No. Recording devices, including phones, dashcams and action cameras, are not permitted and must be disabled. If a built-in camera cannot be turned off, you must confirm it is not recording the inside of the car or the examiner.

### Can my instructor or a family member ride along?

No. Only you and the examiner can be in the car. Others wait in a designated area, and an instructor or translator can help, with consent, at check-in and at the debrief.

# Port Union DriveTest: Road Test Guide for the East Scarborough Centre

URL: https://publicstardrivingschool.com/blog/port-union-drivetest-guide/
Published: 2026-11-19. Updated: 2026-11-19.

Quick answer: Port Union DriveTest is at The Village of Abbey Lane Shopping Centre, 91 Rylander Blvd, Unit 109A, Toronto, and it runs G2 and G road tests Monday to Saturday from 8:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m. The G2 road test costs $53.75 and the G road test costs $91.25, and Ontario asks you to arrive at least 30 minutes before your appointment. Bring a car in good working order, your glasses or contacts if you need them, and plan a ride home if you are testing on a G1.

Port Union is the DriveTest centre in the east end of Scarborough, close to the Pickering border. Many of our students from Scarborough, Pickering and Ajax book it because it is near home or has an earlier opening than other centres. This guide covers the practical side: where it is, when road tests run, what they cost, what to bring and how to prepare.

## Where is the Port Union DriveTest centre?

DriveTest lists the centre as Toronto Port Union at:

The Village of Abbey Lane Shopping Centre, 91 Rylander Blvd, Unit 109A, Toronto, M1B 5M5

It is inside a shopping plaza, so you park in the plaza lot and walk in to check in. Plazas get busy on weekends, so leave a few extra minutes to find a spot. If you are driving in from Pickering, Ajax or Whitby, check traffic before you leave so you are not rushing on test day.

## Port Union hours and road tests offered

According to DriveTest's alphabetical centre list, Port Union offers road tests for Class G2 and Class G only. If you need a motorcycle or commercial road test, you will have to book a different centre.

| Service | Days | Hours |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Inside services (licences, knowledge tests) | Monday to Friday | 7:00 a.m. to 7:00 p.m. |
| Inside services | Saturday | 8:30 a.m. to 5:00 p.m. |
| Road test appointments | Monday to Saturday | 8:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m. |

Hours can change for holidays or bad weather, so check the DriveTest service disruptions page (https://drivetest.ca/find-a-drivetest-centre/service-disruptions/) on the morning of your test.

## How much does a road test at Port Union cost?

Road test fees are set by the Government of Ontario and are the same at every DriveTest centre. These are DriveTest's current fees, taxes included:

| Road test | DriveTest fee |
| --- | --- |
| Class G2 road test | $53.75 |
| Class G road test | $91.25 |

Your first G2 road test is already included in the $159.75 G1 licence package you paid when you applied. You pay again for the G road test and for any retest. DriveTest accepts cash, Visa, Mastercard, debit and a few other methods listed on its fees page (https://drivetest.ca/tests/fees/). Ontario's handbook also reminds drivers that the ministry and DriveTest do not charge fees to book road tests, so be careful of sites that do.

## What to bring to your Port Union road test

Ontario's handbook gives the same checklist for the G2 and G road tests:

- A vehicle in good working order. It must be fit, in proper working condition, plated and insured.
- Money for test fees, if you have not prepaid.
- Glasses or contact lenses if you need them to drive.
- Your arrival plan. Arrive at least 30 minutes before your road test appointment.

For the G test, you also need highway driving experience on roads with speed limits of at least 80 km/h, and you complete a Declaration of Highway Driving Experience form before the test. Our G road test highway tips (/blog/g-road-test-highway-tips/) cover how to build that experience.

## Rules for test day

These rules come from Ontario's handbook and apply at every centre, Port Union included:

1. No passengers. Only you and the examiner are in the car. Driving instructors, friends, relatives and translators cannot come along, and no pets either.
2. No driving aids. Automatic parallel parking, lane monitoring, cruise control and back cameras may not be used. Practise with mirrors and shoulder checks.
3. The examiner cannot coach you. Ask any questions before you start driving.
4. Plan your ride home. If you are a G1 driver, an accompanying driver must come with you to the centre. If you are a G2 driver, be ready to get home another way in case you do not pass.
5. Cancel early. If you cancel or reschedule with less than 48 hours notice, or miss the test, your prepaid fee is not refunded.
6. Bring a ready car. If the car does not meet ministry standards, the test is declared out-of-order and you lose 50% of the fee.

For a walk-through of check-in and the vehicle check, our Metro East DriveTest guide (/blog/metro-east-drivetest-tips/) explains the steps, which are the same at every centre.

## How to prepare for driving around Port Union

The centre sits in a mostly residential part of east Scarborough, with quieter neighbourhood streets close to busier main roads. That mix is good news: you can practise most of what the test asks for nearby. Focus on:

- Residential streets: full stops at stop signs, lower speed limits, and watching for pedestrians and children near schools and parks.
- Busier main roads: lane changes with a mirror and shoulder check every time, and steady speed control.
- Intersections: left turns on a green light, waiting in the right spot and turning into the correct lane.
- Parking and reversing: the handbook lists parallel parking and reversing as skills you will be tested on. See our parallel parking guide (/blog/parallel-parking-road-test-ontario/) and our three-point turn and roadside stop guide (/blog/three-point-turn-roadside-stop-road-test/).

There is no official ranking of "easy" DriveTest centres, and we will not invent one. Choose the centre whose roads you can practise on most. Students in east Scarborough and Pickering often find Port Union convenient, while others book Metro East (/blog/metro-east-drivetest-tips/) or Oshawa (/blog/oshawa-drivetest-tips/).

## If you do not pass

The examiner gives you a full report at the end of the test and explains any mistakes. If you do not pass, Ontario says you must wait at least 10 days before your next test. Use that time to work on the exact points on your report. Our guide to G2 road test automatic fails (/blog/g2-road-test-automatic-fails/) explains the mistakes that end a test early.

## Road test packages for Port Union

Our road test packages include our instructor's car for the test, a warm-up drive first, and pick-up and drop-off in Scarborough, North York, Pickering, Ajax, Whitby and Oshawa. Prices are before and after 13% HST:

| Package | Price |
| --- | --- |
| G2: 2 hours + road test | $200 + HST ($226.00) |
| G2: 3 hours + road test | $250 + HST ($282.50) |
| G2: 5 hours + road test | $330 + HST ($372.90) |
| G: 2 hours + road test | $250 + HST ($282.50) |
| G: 3 hours + road test | $300 + HST ($339.00) |

The DriveTest road test fee is separate and paid to DriveTest. For every package, see our driving lesson cost guide (/blog/driving-lessons-cost-ontario/), and for general tips read how to pass your G2 road test on the first try (/blog/how-to-pass-g2-road-test/).

## Frequently asked questions

### What road tests does Port Union DriveTest offer?

DriveTest lists Port Union for Class G2 and Class G road tests. Motorcycle and commercial road tests are not offered there.

### What are the Port Union DriveTest road test hours?

Road test appointments run Monday to Saturday from 8:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m. Inside services run Monday to Friday 7:00 a.m. to 7:00 p.m. and Saturday 8:30 a.m. to 5:00 p.m.

### How early should I arrive for my road test at Port Union?

Ontario's road test checklist says to arrive at least 30 minutes before your appointment.

### Can my driving instructor ride with me during the test?

No. Only you and the examiner can be in the car. Your instructor can drive you there, warm you up and wait for you.

### Is Port Union easier than other DriveTest centres?

There is no official pass rate ranking by centre. The best choice is a centre whose roads you can practise on before your test.

# Winter Driving Tips for New Drivers in Ontario

URL: https://publicstardrivingschool.com/blog/winter-driving-tips-new-drivers/
Published: 2026-11-18. Updated: 2026-11-18.

Quick answer: To drive safely in an Ontario winter as a new driver, put four matching winter tires on your car (Ontario says they can shorten braking distances by as much as 25%), keep your fuel tank at least half full, carry a winter survival kit, and clear all snow and ice from your windows, lights, mirrors and roof before you leave. On the road, slow down, leave much more space, skip cruise control on slippery pavement, and never pass a working snowplow. If you skid, release the brakes and steer gently where you want to go.

Your first winter behind the wheel can feel like learning to drive all over again. Slush fills the lanes, ice forms at stop lines and snowbanks hide the corners. For G1 and G2 drivers in Scarborough, North York, Pickering, Ajax, Whitby and Oshawa, the first big snowfall often arrives just as road tests are booked.

Winter driving is a skill like any other. This guide covers how to get your car ready, what to do before every trip, and how to drive when the roads turn slippery. The safety advice follows Ontario's official winter driving page (https://www.ontario.ca/page/winter-driving), checked in November 2026.

## How do I get my car ready for winter in Ontario?

Do this before the first snowfall. Ontario recommends:

- A maintenance checkup so your battery, brakes, wipers and lights are ready.
- A fuel tank at least half full. It helps reduce moisture in the fuel system and adds weight to the car.
- An ice scraper and washer fluid rated to minus 40°C.
- A winter survival kit that stays in the car all season.

### What to put in a winter emergency kit

| Item | Why it helps |
| --- | --- |
| Charged phone | Call for help if you slide off the road |
| Water and non-perishable food | You may wait a while in a storm |
| Flashlight | Signal for help and check the car at night |
| Blanket and warm clothes | Stay warm if the engine is off |
| Jumper cables | Cold weather is hard on batteries |
| Shovel | Dig out after a plow or a snowbank |
| Traction mats or sand | Get moving again on ice |
| Candles and a lighter or matches | Light and a little heat |

## Do I need winter tires in Ontario?

Winter tires are one of the best safety upgrades a new driver can make. Ontario says they improve traction and control in frost, snow and ice, and can shorten braking distances by as much as 25%. Some insurers also give a discount, so ask your provider.

- Install four winter tires. Never mix different types of tires on one car.
- Look for the three-peak mountain snowflake symbol on the sidewall.
- All-season tires are not winter tires. They can start to lose grip at around 7°C.
- Studded tires are not allowed in Southern Ontario for most drivers, so they are not an option in the GTA and Durham Region.
- Check tire pressure often. Cold weather lowers it.

## What should I do before driving in snow?

1. Check the forecast. If a storm is coming and the trip can wait, delay it.
2. Check road conditions on Ontario 511 (https://www.ontario.ca/511), which also shows where plows are on provincial highways.
3. Clear the whole car: every window, your headlights and taillights, the mirrors and the roof. Roof snow can slide onto your windshield when you brake.
4. Let the windows defog fully so you can check your blind spots.

## How do new drivers drive safely on snow and ice?

### Slow down and leave space

Ontario notes that many winter collisions happen because drivers are going too fast for the road. The posted limit is a maximum for a dry day, not a target in a snowstorm. It also takes longer to stop on a slippery road, so leave a much bigger gap to the car ahead and start braking earlier for lights and stop signs.

### Be smooth with every control

Hard braking, quick acceleration and sudden gear changes can all cause a skid. Steer gently on curves and press the brake and gas gradually. Ontario also advises against cruise control on wet, snowy or icy pavement, because it reduces your reaction time and control.

### Watch for black ice

Winter asphalt usually looks grey and white. If the road ahead looks black and shiny, it could be ice. Bridges, overpasses and shaded spots freeze first, so ease off the gas before you reach them.

### See and be seen

In poor visibility or whiteouts, turn on your full lighting system so others can see you. If conditions become dangerous, pull over somewhere safe and wait.

## What do I do if my car starts to skid?

1. Take your foot off the brake.
2. Look and steer where you want to go, not at what you are worried about hitting.
3. Keep your steering small. Ontario warns that steering too far can make the car spin.
4. Once the tires grip again, straighten out and slow down gently.

Most skids start when a driver brakes or turns too hard for the grip available, so speed and space are still the best prevention.

## How should I drive near snowplows?

Plows and salt trucks with flashing blue lights work the highways before, during and after storms. Ontario's advice:

- Stay well back from working snowplows and other maintenance vehicles.
- Never pass a working snowplow. Blowing snow and the ridge a plow leaves behind can hide the road and other vehicles.
- Be patient. Roads are plowed in sections, so you usually will not be stuck behind a plow for more than 20 to 30 minutes.

If highway driving is new to you, our G road test highway tips (/blog/g-road-test-highway-tips/) cover merging and lane changes on the 401 and beyond.

## Can winter affect my G2 or G road test?

Yes. The skills examiners look for do not change, but they get harder: full stops behind the line, smooth braking and good space cushions all take more care on slush. Severe weather can also affect test schedules, so if a storm hits on test day, check drivetest.ca (https://www.drivetest.ca) or contact DriveTest about your appointment.

If your test is in the winter months, practise in winter conditions first. Our guide on how to pass the G2 road test (/blog/how-to-pass-g2-road-test/) lists the habits examiners check, and the G2 automatic fails list (/blog/g2-road-test-automatic-fails/) shows mistakes that are easier to make on a slippery road, such as rolling through a stop.

## Practise winter driving with an instructor

Nothing replaces practice with someone calm beside you. A winter lesson lets you feel how much longer the car takes to stop and how gently you need to steer on a snowy street or a slushy on ramp.

Public Star Driving School offers one-on-one lessons with free pick-up and drop-off across Scarborough, North York, Pickering, Ajax, Whitby and Oshawa. A one hour G2 lesson is $50 plus HST ($56.50 total). Not sure how much practice you need? See how many driving lessons you need before your G2 (/blog/how-many-driving-lessons-before-g2/), or call (437) 777-4494 to book.

## Frequently asked questions

### Are winter tires mandatory in Ontario?

Ontario's winter driving page recommends winter tires but does not list them as a requirement for passenger cars. They can shorten braking distances by as much as 25%, and many insurers offer a discount.

### Can a G1 or G2 driver drive in snow?

Yes. Winter weather does not change the G1 or G2 rules: G1 drivers still need a fully licensed accompanying driver. Start with quiet streets in light snow before busy roads or highways.

### When should I switch to winter tires?

All-season tires can start to lose grip at around 7°C, so many drivers switch once daytime temperatures regularly drop to about that level, before the first snowfall.

### How much space should I leave in winter?

Leave enough room that you could stop gently if the car ahead stopped suddenly. On ice, that can be several times your normal gap.

# Nervous About Your Road Test? How to Beat Road Test Anxiety

URL: https://publicstardrivingschool.com/blog/road-test-anxiety-tips/
Published: 2026-11-17. Updated: 2026-11-17.

Quick answer: Road test anxiety mostly comes from uncertainty, so the best fix is to remove surprises: practise the exact tasks on the test (roadside stop, three-point turn, parking, lane changes) until they feel routine, drive the roads near your DriveTest centre, and take a mock test with an instructor. On test day, arrive early, take a warm-up drive, breathe slowly before you start, and if you make a small mistake, let it go and keep driving safely, because one minor error rarely decides the result.

Almost everyone feels nervous before a road test. You have a stranger with a clipboard in the passenger seat, a licence on the line and a route you cannot see in advance. A little adrenaline is normal and can even keep you alert. The problem is when nerves make you forget your blind spot check or freeze at a busy left turn.

The good news is that road test anxiety is very fixable. Most of it comes from not knowing what will happen, and you can take most of that unknown away with the right preparation. This guide covers what to do in the weeks before your test, on the morning of the test, and in the car itself.

## Why do I get so nervous before my driving test?

Test nerves usually come from a few predictable places:

- Fear of the unknown. You do not know the route, the examiner or which tasks you will be asked to do.
- Feeling watched. Driving with a family member is different from driving while someone marks every move.
- High stakes. Rebooking costs time and money, and you may need the licence for school or work.
- A past bad experience. A failed test or a near miss can stick with you.

Notice that most of these are about uncertainty, not about your actual driving skill. That is why preparation works so well: the more of the test you have already done many times, the less room there is for nerves.

## How to prepare in the weeks before your road test

### Practise every test task until it is boring

You will not know in advance exactly what the examiner will ask for, so practise all of it. On the G2 road test that means roadside stops and three-point turns (/blog/three-point-turn-roadside-stop-road-test/), parallel parking (/blog/parallel-parking-road-test-ontario/), lane changes, left turns at busy intersections and school zones. The goal is for each task to feel like a routine you could do half asleep. Routines hold up under pressure much better than things you are still thinking through.

### Learn the roads near your test centre

Every DriveTest centre has its own mix of speed changes, school zones and tricky intersections. Driving those streets ahead of time turns the test route from a mystery into familiar ground. Our Metro East DriveTest tips (/blog/metro-east-drivetest-tips/) and Oshawa DriveTest tips (/blog/oshawa-drivetest-tips/) cover two centres our students use most.

### Take a mock road test

A mock test with an instructor is the closest thing to the real experience. Your instructor gives directions the way an examiner would, stays quiet in between, and tells you afterwards exactly what would have cost you marks. Doing this once or twice takes a lot of the shock out of test day.

### Know what actually fails a test

A lot of anxiety comes from imagining that any small slip means instant failure. It does not. Minor mistakes add up on the score sheet, while dangerous actions like rolling a stop sign or an unsafe lane change are what usually end a test. Reading our guide on G2 road test automatic fails (/blog/g2-road-test-automatic-fails/) helps you focus your worry on the few things that really matter.

## What to do on the day of your road test

| When | What to do | Why it helps |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Night before | Get your documents ready and sleep at a normal time | No morning scramble |
| Morning | Eat a light meal and skip extra coffee | Caffeine can make shaky hands worse |
| Before leaving | Plan to arrive early | Rushing raises your heart rate before you start |
| At the centre | Take a short warm-up drive if you can | Your first drive of the day is not the test |
| In the car | Adjust seat and mirrors slowly, then breathe | Gives you a calm moment before you move |

### Use slow breathing before you start

Before you pull away, take a few slow breaths: in through your nose for about four seconds, hold briefly, then out through your mouth a little longer than you breathed in. Slower breathing helps settle your body, and it gives you a moment to set your mirrors and focus.

### Drive in the car you trained in

A car you know removes one more source of stress: you already know where the signals, wipers and hazard lights are, and how the brakes feel. If you do not have a suitable car, our guide to using a rented or driving school car for your road test (/blog/road-test-car-rental-ontario/) explains your options.

## How to stay calm during the test

- Talk yourself through it quietly. Some drivers find it helps to think "mirror, signal, blind spot" before every lane change. It keeps your mind on the job.
- Ask if you did not hear an instruction. Examiners expect this. Asking is far better than guessing.
- Make your checks obvious. Turn your head for blind spots and scan intersections clearly so the examiner can see you doing it.
- Drive at a steady, legal speed. Driving very slowly out of nervousness can count against you too.
- Reset after a mistake. If you miss a check or stop a little far from the line, let it go. Dwelling on it is how one small error turns into three.

## What if I still fail because of nerves?

It happens, and it is not the end of the road. Ask the examiner for your score sheet and look at what was marked. Usually it is one or two habits that showed up under pressure, which a couple of focused lessons can fix. Then rebook when you feel ready, not just as soon as possible. Many confident drivers passed on their second try.

## How Public Star helps nervous drivers

Our instructors work with a lot of first-time and nervous drivers across Ajax, Pickering, Whitby, Oshawa, Scarborough and North York. Lessons are one-on-one, so you can go at your own pace and ask as many questions as you need.

- Single G2 lessons are $50 + HST ($56.50) per hour, good for practising one task you dread.
- Road test bundles include lesson time, a warm-up drive right before the test and the use of our car on test day. Our most popular G2 bundle, 5 hours + road test, is $330 + HST ($372.90).

Not sure how much practice you need? Our guide on how many driving lessons you need before the G2 (/blog/how-many-driving-lessons-before-g2/) helps you judge, and how to pass the G2 road test (/blog/how-to-pass-g2-road-test/) covers the skills examiners look for.

## Frequently asked questions

### Is it normal to be nervous for a road test?

Yes, very. Most people feel some nerves. A small amount keeps you alert. The aim is not to feel nothing, but to be prepared enough that nerves do not change how you drive.

### Can I tell the examiner I am nervous?

Yes. Saying you are a bit nervous is fine and can help you relax. The examiner will still mark the test the same way, so focus on driving safely and making your checks clear.

### Does a warm-up lesson before the test help with nerves?

For many drivers it does. A short drive right before the test settles your hands, reminds you of the car and means the test is not your first time behind the wheel that day.

### What should I do if I make a mistake during the test?

Keep driving safely and do not try to fix the past. One minor error rarely fails a test on its own, but losing focus after it can lead to more mistakes.

### How many lessons do nervous drivers usually need?

It depends on your experience. Drivers who have practised with family often need 3 to 5 hours with an instructor to polish habits, while brand new drivers usually need more.

# Three-Point Turn and Roadside Stop: Ontario Road Test Step by Step

URL: https://publicstardrivingschool.com/blog/three-point-turn-roadside-stop-road-test/
Published: 2026-11-16. Updated: 2026-11-16.

Quick answer: On the Ontario G2 road test, a roadside stop means signalling, slowing steadily and stopping parallel to the curb no more than about 30 centimetres away, then switching your signal off, hazard lights on and setting the parking brake. A three-point turn starts from that stop: left signal, check mirrors and blind spot, steer sharply left across the road, stop, reverse with the wheel sharply right, stop, then drive forward. Use the whole road, reverse only once, and never touch the curb.

The three-point turn and the roadside stop are two of the shortest tasks on the G2 road test, but they are packed with checks that are easy to forget under pressure. The examiner usually asks for them on a quiet residential street, often back to back. This guide follows the official MTO Driver's Handbook so you know exactly what to do and what the examiner is looking for.

## Are the three-point turn and roadside stop on the Ontario road test?

Yes, on the G2 road test (the G1 exit test). They are part of the residential driving section, along with parallel parking.

The G road test (the G2 exit test) does not include them at the moment. The handbook says that until further notice the G test will not include parallel parking, roadside stops, 3-point turns or driving in residential neighbourhoods, because those are already covered on the G2 test. Our G2 vs G road test guide (/blog/g2-vs-g-road-test/) explains what each test covers.

## How to do a roadside stop, step by step

The examiner will say something like "pull over and stop behind the next parked car" or "stop at the side of the road when it is safe." Here is the handbook method, split into the three parts the examiner marks.

### 1. The approach

- Check traffic before you slow down. Look in your mirrors and scan for signs to make sure stopping there is legal. The handbook says a 150 metre gap in traffic in both directions gives you enough space to do it safely.
- Check your right blind spot if a cyclist or pedestrian could pass you on the right.
- Signal before you slow down. If there are driveways or side roads between you and your stopping point with cars waiting to pull out, wait until you pass them so nobody thinks you are turning.
- Slow down steadily. No sudden braking.
- Stop parallel to the curb, not more than about 30 centimetres away. If there is no curb, stop as far off the travelled part of the road as you can. Do not block a driveway or other traffic.

### 2. The stop

- Turn off your signal and turn on your hazard lights.
- Put the car in park and set the parking brake (automatic transmission).

### 3. Resuming

- Release the parking brake and select drive.
- Turn off your hazard lights and turn on your left signal.
- Check your mirrors and your left blind spot just before you pull away.
- Accelerate smoothly back to normal traffic speed, then cancel your signal.

Forgetting to switch from hazards back to the left signal is one of the most common small errors we see. Say it out loud in practice: "hazards off, signal on, mirror, shoulder, go."

## How to do a three-point turn, step by step

A three-point turn is how you turn around on a narrow road. On the test the examiner will ask you to pull over first, so the turn starts from a roadside stop on the right side of the road.

1. Pull over on the right. Use the roadside stop approach above and stop parallel to the curb, no more than 30 centimetres away.
2. Signal left. Turn on your left signal before you start the turn.
3. Check all around. Look in your mirrors and over your left shoulder. Wait until the way is clear in both directions, or traffic has stopped to let you turn.
4. Forward, wheel sharply left. Move slowly and smoothly across the road toward the far curb, turning the wheel fully to the left.
5. Stop before the far curb. Do not touch it. Shift into reverse.
6. Check traffic again. The handbook says to check in both directions every time you stop during the turn.
7. Reverse, wheel sharply right. Look behind you and back up slowly with the wheel turned fully right until the car faces the new direction. Do not reverse over the edge or shoulder of the road or into the curb.
8. Stop, shift to drive, check and go. Check your mirrors, then accelerate smoothly to normal speed.

The handbook's key rule for the test: use the whole road and reverse only once. If you need a fourth or fifth point, it usually means you started too far from the curb or turned the wheel too slowly.

## What the examiner watches

| Task | What the examiner checks |
| --- | --- |
| Roadside stop approach | Mirror check, legal spot, signal timing, steady slowing |
| Roadside stop position | Parallel, about 30 cm or less from the curb, not blocking anything |
| After stopping | Signal off, hazards on, park and parking brake |
| Resuming | Hazards off, left signal, mirrors and left blind spot |
| Three-point turn | Signal, checks at every stop, full road width, one reverse only |
| Car control | Slow, smooth movement, no curb contact |

Most marks on these tasks are lost for missed observation, not for the turn itself. Turn your head on every check so the examiner can see you looking. Our G2 automatic fails guide (/blog/g2-road-test-automatic-fails/) covers the mistakes that can end a test.

## Where you should not make a three-point turn

You will not get to choose the spot on the test, but in everyday driving the handbook says not to make a three-point turn:

- On a curve in the road
- On or near a railway crossing or a hilltop
- Near a bridge or tunnel that blocks your view

The handbook also says the simplest and safest way to turn around is often to drive around the block.

## Common mistakes and how to fix them

- Stopping too far from the curb. More than about 30 centimetres away costs marks and leaves you with less room for the turn. Practise judging the gap with a friend outside the car.
- Leaving the signal on after stopping. Switch to hazard lights as soon as you stop.
- Checking only the mirrors. Shoulder checks are required before pulling out and before the turn.
- Rushing the steering. Turn the wheel fully while the car creeps forward, so you reach the far side at the right angle.
- Touching the curb. Stop a little short. A gap is fine; contact is not.
- Forgetting the parking brake. It is part of the stop, even for a short pause.

## How to practise

Find a quiet, wide residential street with good sightlines in both directions. Practise the roadside stop until the sequence is automatic, then add the three-point turn from that stop. Practise in the same car you will test in, because turning circles differ. If you also need work on parking, see our parallel parking guide (/blog/parallel-parking-road-test-ontario/), since all three tasks usually come up in the same part of the test.

## Practise with a Public Star instructor

Our instructors run these exact tasks on residential streets similar to the ones around DriveTest centres, and every road test package includes the instructor's car for the test and a warm-up drive. We offer free pick-up and drop-off in Scarborough, North York, Pickering, Ajax, Whitby and Oshawa.

| G2 package | Price |
| --- | --- |
| 1 hour lesson | $50 + HST ($56.50) |
| 2 hours + road test | $200 + HST ($226.00) |
| 3 hours + road test | $250 + HST ($282.50) |
| 4 hours + road test | $300 + HST ($339.00) |
| 5 hours + road test | $330 + HST ($372.90) |
| 10 hours + road test | $550 + HST ($621.50) |

For a full test day plan, read how to pass the G2 road test (/blog/how-to-pass-g2-road-test/).

## Frequently asked questions

### Is the three-point turn on the G test in Ontario?

Not currently. The handbook says the G road test will not include 3-point turns, roadside stops or parallel parking until further notice, because they are covered on the G2 test.

### How close to the curb should I stop for a roadside stop?

Parallel to the curb and not more than about 30 centimetres away. If there is no curb, stop as far off the travelled part of the road as possible.

### Do I use hazard lights during a roadside stop?

Yes. Once you have stopped, turn off your signal and turn on your hazard lights. Before you pull away, turn the hazards off and signal left.

### What if I cannot finish the three-point turn in three moves?

The handbook says to use the whole road and reverse only once, so extra moves can cost marks. Starting close to the right curb and turning the wheel fully helps you finish in three.

### Should I check my blind spot during the turn?

Yes. Check your mirrors and blind spot before you start, and check traffic in both directions each time you stop during the turn.

# How to Parallel Park for Your Road Test in Ontario

URL: https://publicstardrivingschool.com/blog/parallel-parking-road-test-ontario/
Published: 2026-11-15. Updated: 2026-11-15.

Quick answer: Parallel parking is part of the Ontario G2 road test (the G1 exit test), not the G test. Find a space about one and a half times your car's length, stop beside the car in front with your rear bumpers lined up, then reverse slowly with the wheel turned fully toward the curb, straighten once you see the other car's rear corner, and turn fully toward the road to finish parallel. Check your mirrors and blind spot before you start, keep it slow, and never touch the curb.

Parallel parking is the manoeuvre students worry about most before a G2 road test. The good news is that it follows a set method, and the Ontario Driver's Handbook spells it out. Once you know the reference points and practise them, it becomes routine. This guide walks through the steps, the checks examiners look for, and the mistakes that cost marks.

## Is parallel parking on the Ontario road test?

Yes, on the first road test. Ontario's licensing page lists parallel parking among the skills checked on the G2 road test (the G1 exit test), along with 3-point turns, stopping, lane changes and driving in residential neighbourhoods.

The G road test (the G2 exit test) currently does not include parallel parking, roadside stops, 3-point turns or residential driving, because those are already covered on the G2 test. If you have passed your G2, you can focus on highway and expressway skills instead. Our G2 vs G road test guide (/blog/g2-vs-g-road-test/) explains the difference in detail.

## Step by step: the MTO parallel parking method

These steps follow the official handbook. Practise them in this order until you do them without thinking.

1. Find the right space. Look for a gap about one and a half times the length of your car, on the right side of the road in the direction of traffic.
2. Signal and check behind you. Turn on your right signal early, check your mirrors, and slow down gently so drivers behind know you are stopping.
3. Stop alongside the car in front of the space. Pull up parallel to it, leaving a gap between the two cars (the handbook's road test section says at least 60 centimetres). Stop when your rear bumper lines up with that car's rear bumper.
4. Look all around, then reverse slowly. Check your mirrors and both blind spots, shift into reverse, and turn the steering wheel fully toward the curb as you start to back up.
5. Straighten the wheels. When you can see the outside rear corner of the car in front of the space, straighten your wheels and keep reversing slowly.
6. Turn toward the road to finish. Turn the steering wheel fully toward the road so the car swings in line with the curb.
7. Adjust if needed. If you are not parallel, drive forward a little to straighten up. Do not hit the curb or the cars around you.
8. Secure the car. Set the parking brake and put the car in park.

When the examiner asks you to move on, signal left, check your mirror and blind spot, and pull out only when there is a safe gap.

## What the examiner watches during parallel parking

Car control matters, but observation matters just as much. On test day the examiner is checking that you:

| What they check | What it looks like |
| --- | --- |
| Signalling | Right signal on before you stop beside the other car |
| Observation | Mirror and blind spot checks before you reverse and before you pull out |
| Speed | Slow, controlled reversing, no sudden jerks |
| Position | Close to the curb and parallel, without touching it |
| Smoothness | A small number of corrections, not repeated back and forth |
| Safety | Yielding to pedestrians, cyclists and cars while you manoeuvre |

A common surprise: many students lose marks on parallel parking for not looking, not for a crooked finish. Turn your head and look out the rear window while you reverse, not only at the mirrors or a backup camera.

## Common parallel parking mistakes

These are the mistakes our instructors correct most often in the weeks before a road test:

- Reversing too fast. Speed makes every small error bigger. Creep back at walking pace or slower.
- Turning the wheel too late or too early. Use the reference point: the outside rear corner of the car in front. That is your cue to straighten.
- Hitting or climbing the curb. A light touch costs marks. Mounting the curb is treated as a serious error, as we explain in our G2 automatic fails guide (/blog/g2-road-test-automatic-fails/).
- Forgetting the blind spot. Cyclists and pedestrians can appear beside you while you reverse.
- Starting too far from the parked car. A big sideways gap leaves you far from the curb at the end.
- Giving up and trying again from scratch. It is usually better to make one small forward correction than to pull out and start over.

## How to practise parallel parking

Practice turns the steps into muscle memory. A few ideas that work well:

- Start in an empty lot. Use two pylons, recycling bins or cardboard boxes to mark a space. You can make mistakes without risk.
- Move to a quiet residential street. Choose a road with little traffic and one or two parked cars, at a time when it is calm.
- Repeat the same reference points every time. Line up your bumpers, wheel fully toward the curb, straighten at the corner, wheel fully toward the road.
- Practise in the car you will test in. Every car has a different length and turning circle. If you test in your instructor's car, practise in it too.
- Practise both sides on one-way streets. Ontario allows parking on both sides of a one-way road unless signs say otherwise, so be ready for either.

Most students need several focused sessions before parallel parking feels easy. Our guide on how many driving lessons you need before your G2 (/blog/how-many-driving-lessons-before-g2/) can help you plan. The other residential tasks on the same test are covered in our three-point turn and roadside stop guide (/blog/three-point-turn-roadside-stop-road-test/).

## Parking rules to remember

Parallel parking well is only half of it. You also need to choose a legal spot. The handbook says, among other rules, that you should not park:

- Within 3 metres of a fire hydrant
- Within 9 metres of an intersection, or 15 metres if it has traffic lights
- Within 15 metres of the nearest rail of a level railway crossing
- In a way that blocks a sidewalk, crosswalk, driveway or another parked vehicle

On a hill, turn your front wheels toward the curb when facing downhill, and away from the curb (toward the road) when facing uphill with a curb. That way the curb stops the car if it rolls.

## Practise with a Public Star instructor

Our instructors practise parallel parking on the same kinds of residential streets you will see near your DriveTest centre, using the exact reference points above. Every road test package includes the instructor's car for the test and a warm-up drive first, with free pick-up and drop-off in Scarborough, North York, Pickering, Ajax, Whitby and Oshawa.

| G2 package | Price |
| --- | --- |
| 1 hour lesson | $50 + HST ($56.50) |
| 2 hours + road test | $200 + HST ($226.00) |
| 3 hours + road test | $250 + HST ($282.50) |
| 5 hours + road test | $330 + HST ($372.90) |
| 10 hours + road test | $550 + HST ($621.50) |

For the full test day plan, read our guide on how to pass the G2 road test (/blog/how-to-pass-g2-road-test/).

## Frequently asked questions

### Is parallel parking on the G test in Ontario?

Not currently. Ontario says the G road test does not include parallel parking, roadside stops or 3-point turns, because they are already covered on the G2 road test.

### How big a space do I need to parallel park?

The Ontario Driver's Handbook recommends a space about one and a half times the length of your vehicle.

### Can I fail the G2 test for bad parallel parking?

Small errors such as one extra correction are marked and added up. A dangerous action, like reversing without looking or hitting another car, can end the test.

### Can I use a backup camera during the road test?

A camera can help, but do not rely on it alone. Examiners expect you to turn and look behind you and check your blind spots while reversing.

### How close to the curb should I be?

The handbook does not give an exact number for parallel parking, but you should end up close to the curb and parallel to it without touching it. For a roadside stop, the handbook says to stop no more than about 30 centimetres from the curb.

# G2 Licence Rules and Restrictions in Ontario: What You Can and Cannot Do

URL: https://publicstardrivingschool.com/blog/g2-licence-rules-ontario/
Published: 2026-11-14. Updated: 2026-11-14.

Quick answer: With a G2 licence in Ontario you can drive alone on all roads, including 400-series highways, at any time of day, but you must keep a zero blood alcohol level, have no drugs in your system and carry only as many passengers as there are working seatbelts. If you are 19 or under, between midnight and 5 a.m. you can carry only one passenger aged 19 or under in your first six months on a G2, and up to three after that. Breaking G2 rules can bring a 30 day suspension for a first offence, 90 days for a second, and loss of your novice licence for a third.

Passing your G2 road test is a big moment: for the first time, you can drive without an experienced driver beside you. But a G2 is still a novice licence, and Ontario keeps several rules in place until you pass your G test. This guide explains every G2 restriction, what happens if you break one, and how to get through the 12 months safely. It is written for new drivers in Scarborough, North York, Pickering, Ajax, Whitby and Oshawa, but the rules apply across Ontario.

All of the rules below come from ontario.ca (https://www.ontario.ca/page/get-g-drivers-licence-new-drivers) and are current as of November 2026. Rules can change, so check the official pages if you are unsure.

## What can you do with a G2 licence in Ontario?

Compared with a G1, a G2 gives you a lot more freedom. Ontario says G2 drivers can drive:

- without another experienced driver in the car,
- on all Ontario roads, including 400-series highways and high-speed expressways,
- at any time of the day, in most cases.

That is why the G2 stage is the best time to build real highway experience before your G test. Our G road test highway tips (/blog/g-road-test-highway-tips/) explain what to practise.

## G2 restrictions at a glance

| Rule | Who it applies to |
| --- | --- |
| Zero blood alcohol level | All G2 drivers |
| No drugs, including cannabis, in your system | All G2 drivers |
| Only as many passengers as working seatbelts | All G2 drivers |
| Midnight to 5 a.m.: only one passenger aged 19 or under (first six months) | G2 drivers aged 19 or under |
| Midnight to 5 a.m.: up to three passengers aged 19 or under (after six months) | G2 drivers aged 19 or under |
| No hand-held phone use while driving | All drivers, with tougher penalties for novices |

## Zero tolerance for alcohol and drugs

Ontario's zero tolerance law says you cannot have any alcohol in your system if you hold a G1, G2, M1 or M2 licence, at any age. The same applies to all drivers aged 21 or under, even with a full G. The rule also covers cannabis and other drugs: Ontario says young and novice drivers must have no alcohol and no drugs in their system when they drive.

Ontario lists these penalties for young and novice drivers who break zero tolerance, on top of any other impaired driving charges:

| Offence | Immediate suspension | Penalty | Other |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| First time | 7 days | $250 | 8 hour education course |
| Second time | 14 days | $350 | 16 hour treatment program |
| Third time | 30 days | $450 | 16 hour treatment program and a 6 month ignition interlock |

If you are convicted, the fine can be $60 to $1,000, and your licence can be suspended for a further 30 or 90 days or cancelled. A reinstatement fee also applies each time a licence is suspended. The simple answer: if you have had anything at all, do not drive.

## G2 passenger rules

Every G2 driver must carry only as many passengers as there are working seatbelts. No exceptions.

If you are 19 or under, there is an extra rule between midnight and 5 a.m.:

1. First six months on your G2: only one passenger aged 19 or under.
2. After six months: up to three passengers aged 19 or under.

These late-night limits do not apply if a fully licensed driver with at least four years of experience is in the car, or if your passengers are immediate family members, such as a brother or sister.

## Phones and distracted driving on a G2

Ontario's distracted driving law applies to everyone, but novice drivers face harsher consequences. You cannot hold a phone or other device while driving, including when you are stopped in traffic or at a red light. You can use a hands-free device only to turn it on and off, and a mounted phone only to touch a button to make, answer or end a call.

The fine is $615 if settled out of court, and more if you are summoned to court. Novice drivers do not get demerit points for this offence. Instead, Ontario says G1 and G2 drivers face:

- a 30 day licence suspension for a first conviction,
- a 90 day licence suspension for a second conviction,
- cancellation of your licence and removal from the graduated licensing system for a third conviction, which means starting over.

Set your GPS and music before you pull out, and put your phone out of reach.

## Demerit points for G2 drivers

Novice drivers reach suspension much sooner than fully licensed drivers. According to Ontario's demerit point page (https://www.ontario.ca/page/understanding-demerit-points):

| Demerit points | What happens to a novice driver |
| --- | --- |
| 2 to 5 | Warning letter |
| 6 to 8 | Second warning letter |
| 9 or more | 60 day licence suspension |

Points stay on your record for two years from the offence date. A fully licensed driver, by comparison, is not suspended until 15 points.

## Escalating penalties for novice drivers

Ontario also has escalating penalties for G1 and G2 drivers who are convicted of breaking graduated licensing rules, or of a Highway Traffic Act offence worth four or more demerit points:

- First offence: 30 day suspension.
- Second offence: 90 day suspension.
- Third offence: you lose your novice licence and must start again, taking all tests and paying all fees. You also lose any time credit, including the time saved from a driver education course.

Losing your G2 can set you back many months, so these rules are worth taking seriously.

## How long do you keep a G2?

You hold your G2 for at least 12 months before you can take the G road test. Ontario gives you up to five years to finish the whole process from G1 to G, or you have to start over. Our G1 to G licence timeline (/blog/g1-to-g-licence-timeline-ontario/) shows how the dates fit together, and the G2 vs G road test (/blog/g2-vs-g-road-test/) comparison explains what the next test adds.

## Tips for a smooth G2 year

- Drive often, not just on weekends. The 12 months are meant for experience, so use them.
- Get highway practice early. Start with quiet times on the 401 or 412 before rush hour.
- Prepare for your first winter. Our winter driving tips for new drivers (/blog/winter-driving-tips-new-drivers/) cover winter tires, black ice and skids.
- Keep a clean record. Even two demerit points trigger a warning letter.
- Plan late-night trips. If you are 19 or under, count passengers before you leave after midnight.
- Book a refresher before your G test. A lesson or two helps you fix habits that crept in.

If you want help, our G lessons start at $60 + HST ($67.80) an hour, and our 3 hours + road test G package is $300 + HST ($339.00), which includes our car for the test and a warm-up drive. Still waiting for your G2 test? Read how to pass the G2 road test on the first try (/blog/how-to-pass-g2-road-test/) and the G2 automatic fails list (/blog/g2-road-test-automatic-fails/).

## Frequently asked questions

### Can I drive on the highway with a G2 in Ontario?

Yes. G2 drivers can drive on all Ontario roads, including 400-series highways and high-speed expressways, without another driver in the car.

### Can a G2 driver drink any alcohol before driving?

No. G2 drivers must keep a zero blood alcohol level and have no drugs, including cannabis, in their system.

### How many passengers can I have with a G2?

Only as many as there are working seatbelts. If you are 19 or under, between midnight and 5 a.m. you can carry one passenger aged 19 or under in your first six months, and up to three after that, unless an experienced driver is with you or the passengers are immediate family.

### What happens if I get caught on my phone with a G2?

You face a $615 fine if settled out of court and a 30 day suspension for a first conviction, 90 days for a second, and cancellation of your licence for a third.

### How many demerit points can a G2 driver have?

A warning letter comes at 2 points, a second at 6, and a 60 day suspension at 9 or more.

---

# Converting a Foreign Driver's Licence in Ontario: A Newcomer's Guide

URL: https://publicstardrivingschool.com/blog/foreign-licence-exchange-ontario/
Published: 2026-11-13. Updated: 2026-11-13.

Quick answer: You can drive in Ontario on a valid licence from another country for 60 days, and after that you need an Ontario licence. If your licence is from another Canadian province, a U.S. state or one of the countries with an exchange agreement (such as Australia, France, Germany, Great Britain, Japan, South Korea or Ukraine), you can apply to exchange it at a DriveTest centre. From any other country, you take the vision test, knowledge test and G2 road test, wait at least 12 months, then take the G road test, and you can get credit for up to one year of driving experience with a valid foreign licence and a letter of authentication.

Moving to Ontario comes with a long to-do list, and getting the right driver's licence is near the top for most newcomers. The good news: your driving experience back home still counts for something. How much it counts depends on where your licence comes from. This guide walks through the rules as ontario.ca explains them, plus what we see helps newcomers pass their road tests in Ajax, Scarborough and across Durham Region.

## How long can you drive in Ontario on a foreign licence?

According to ontario.ca, you can use a valid licence from another province, state or country for 60 days. After 60 days, you need to switch to an Ontario driver's licence.

Sixty days goes by quickly when you are also finding a home, a job and a school for your kids. Start the licence process in your first few weeks, especially if you will need to book road tests.

## Which countries can exchange their licence in Ontario?

Ontario lets you exchange an out-of-province licence if you are relocating from:

- any Canadian province or territory
- the Canadian Armed Forces
- a U.S. state (U.S. territories and protectorates are not included)
- Australia, Austria, Belgium, Croatia, Denmark, France, Germany, Great Britain, Hungary, the Isle of Man, Japan, South Korea, Kosovo, New Zealand, Northern Ireland, the Republic of Ireland, Switzerland, Taiwan or Ukraine

Even from one of these places, the exchange is not automatic. Ontario says the process depends on where you were licensed, your licence class and your driving experience, and that you might still need to take a knowledge test or road test. Check the exchange details on drivetest.ca for your exact situation before you go.

## What if your country is not on the exchange list?

Most newcomers to the Greater Toronto Area come from countries without an exchange agreement, including India, Pakistan, the Philippines, China, Iran, Nigeria and many others. If that is you, ontario.ca lists these steps:

1. Pass the vision test and the knowledge test at a DriveTest centre.
2. Pass the G2 road test.
3. Wait at least 12 months before you attempt the G road test.
4. Pass the G road test to get your full G licence.

Since July 1, 2026, you can get credit for up to one year of driving experience by showing a valid, original foreign driver's licence and an authentication document. Ask DriveTest how that credit applies to your timeline when you apply.

For a full picture of how the levels fit together, see our G1 to G licence timeline (/blog/g1-to-g-licence-timeline-ontario/).

## What is a letter of authentication?

To get credit for your foreign experience, you need a letter of authentication. Ontario says it must be:

- an official letter from the foreign government or agency that issued your licence
- a confirmation that your licence is authentic
- written in English or French

Request this letter early. Depending on the country, it can take weeks to arrive, and you may need family back home to help.

## Documents to bring to DriveTest

You apply in person at a DriveTest centre or at ServiceOntario Bay and College in Toronto. Bring:

| Document | Notes from ontario.ca |
| --- | --- |
| Identity documents | Originals showing your legal name and date of birth |
| Foreign driver's licence | Original and valid, with a visible expiry date |
| Translation | Needed if the licence is not in English or French |
| Letter of authentication | Needed to get credit for driving experience |
| Proof of driving experience | Original supporting documents in English or French |

Translations: the translation must be done by a certified translator and dated within six months of your application. Ontario accepts translations from non-Canadian embassies, consulates or high commissioner's offices, but not other translators from the country that issued the licence. Translators must provide proof of their credentials.

Since May 11, 2026, Class G applicants also declare that Ontario is their primary place of residence and that their presence in Canada is legal.

DriveTest charges fees for the licence application, the knowledge test and each road test. Check the current list on drivetest.ca before you go, since we cannot confirm amounts here.

## Why experienced drivers still fail the Ontario road test

This is the part that surprises many newcomers. You may have driven safely for years, yet Ontario examiners mark specific habits that are normal elsewhere. The ones we see most often:

- Rolling stops. Ontario expects a full stop behind the line at every stop sign.
- Shoulder checks. Examiners watch for a head turn before every lane change, merge and turn from the curb. Mirrors alone are not enough.
- Right turns on red. They are allowed, but only after a complete stop and when it is safe.
- School buses and pedestrians. The rules around stopped school buses and crosswalks are strict.
- Speed in school zones and residential streets. Posted limits change often, and examiners notice.

None of this is hard to fix, but old habits are automatic. A few lessons with an instructor who knows the test routes usually clears them up. Our G2 automatic fails list (/blog/g2-road-test-automatic-fails/) covers the mistakes that end a test early.

## How many lessons does an experienced newcomer need?

Less than a brand new driver, in most cases. Experienced drivers often need only a couple of hours to learn Ontario test habits, then a run through the test route. Our guide on how many lessons you need before the G2 (/blog/how-many-driving-lessons-before-g2/) goes into more detail.

Here are our packages that newcomers book most often (prices include 13% HST):

| Package | Price | Total with HST |
| --- | --- | --- |
| G2: 1 hour lesson | $50 | $56.50 |
| G2: 2 hours + road test | $200 | $226.00 |
| G2: 5 hours + road test | $330 | $372.90 |
| G: 2 hours + road test | $250 | $282.50 |
| G: 3 hours + road test | $300 | $339.00 |

Road test packages include the use of our car on test day. If you do not own a car in Canada yet, that matters: see renting a car for your road test (/blog/road-test-car-rental-ontario/). We offer free pick-up and drop-off in Ajax, Pickering, Whitby, Oshawa, Scarborough and North York.

## Frequently asked questions

### Can I drive in Ontario with an international driving permit?

Ontario's exchange page says you can drive on a valid licence from another country for 60 days, then you need an Ontario licence. It does not describe the international driving permit, so check with DriveTest or your insurer about your situation.

### Is India on Ontario's licence exchange list?

No. India is not on the list ontario.ca gives. Drivers from India take the vision test, knowledge test and G2 road test, and can get credit for up to one year of experience with a valid licence and a letter of authentication.

### Do I need to take the knowledge test if I have driven for years?

If your licence is from a country without an exchange agreement, yes. Ontario lists the vision test and knowledge test as the first steps. Drivers from exchange countries may or may not need tests, depending on their circumstances.

### Where can I get my licence translated?

Ontario accepts translations from a certified translator, including non-Canadian embassies, consulates and high commissioner's offices. The translation must be dated within six months of your application.

### Can I use a driving school car for my road test?

Yes. All our road test packages include the car on test day, plus a warm-up lesson before the test.

# Driving Lessons in North York: A Guide for New Drivers

URL: https://publicstardrivingschool.com/blog/driving-lessons-north-york/
Published: 2026-11-12. Updated: 2026-11-12.

Quick answer: Driving lessons in North York are one-on-one sessions with a certified instructor who picks you up from home, school or work and builds from quiet residential streets up to Yonge Street, Sheppard Avenue and Highway 401. At Public Star, a single G2 lesson is $50 + HST ($56.50), a G lesson is $60 + HST ($67.80), and the G2 5 hours plus road test bundle is $330 + HST ($372.90), including a warm-up and our car on test day.

North York is the busiest of the six cities our instructors teach in. It has some of the heaviest traffic in Ontario, a stretch of Highway 401 that many new drivers find intimidating, and plenty of quiet side streets where you can learn the basics first. This guide explains how lessons in North York work, which roads help you prepare for your road test and what it all costs.

## What does a driving lesson in North York look like?

Every lesson is one-on-one, so the full hour is yours. Your instructor picks you up from your home, school or workplace in North York, whether that is near York University, a subway station on Yonge Street or a quiet street in Don Mills, and plans each lesson around what you need next.

Your first lesson usually includes:

- Getting set up: seat, mirrors and steering wheel position before you move.
- A quick assessment: starts, stops, turns and lane position on quiet streets.
- Honest feedback: what you already do well and which habits would cost marks on a road test.
- A plan: a realistic estimate of how many lessons you need and what each one will cover.

Each lesson after that builds on the last one. In North York, that usually means extra time on the skills busy city traffic demands: scanning for pedestrians and cyclists, choosing the right lane early and making left turns at large intersections without rushing.

## What licence do you need to start lessons in North York?

You need a G1 licence, which you get by passing a vision test and the written knowledge test at a DriveTest centre. Once you have it, you can start lessons with a certified driving instructor right away.

While you hold a G1 in Ontario, you must:

- Keep a zero blood alcohol level.
- Not drive between midnight and 5 a.m.
- Not drive on 400-series highways or high-speed expressways such as the 401.
- Always drive with a fully licensed driver who has at least four years of driving experience, and who is the only other person in the front seat.

There is one important exception. When you drive with a driving instructor certified in Ontario, you can drive on any road. For North York drivers that matters a lot, because Highway 401, Highway 404 and the Don Valley Parkway all run through or beside the city. A lesson is the only way to practise on them while you hold a G1.

## Local roads worth practising on in North York

North York packs almost every kind of driving into a small area. Lessons usually move through it in stages:

| Stage | Type of road | What you practise |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Beginner | Residential streets in neighbourhoods like Willowdale, Bayview Village and Newtonbrook | Steering control, full stops, speed control, scanning for children and pedestrians |
| Building up | Main roads such as Bathurst Street, Bayview Avenue and Leslie Street | Left turns at lights, lane changes, following distance |
| Busier traffic | Yonge Street, Sheppard Avenue and Finch Avenue | Heavy traffic, buses, plaza entrances, pedestrians and cyclists |
| G test prep | Highway 401, Highway 404 and the Don Valley Parkway | Merging, exiting and changing lanes at highway speed |

DriveTest does not publish its test routes, so memorizing streets is not the goal. The goal is to feel calm on every type of road, so nothing on test day feels new. A driver who can handle Yonge and Sheppard at rush hour is usually well prepared for any test route.

## Driving on Highway 401 through North York

The 401 through North York has express and collector lanes, frequent exits and heavy traffic for much of the day. For a G road test, you need to merge, change lanes and exit smoothly at highway speed. We start highway practice only once you are comfortable on busy city roads, and we usually begin outside rush hour.

The skills we focus on:

1. Building speed on the ramp so you merge at the speed of traffic, not below it.
2. Checking mirrors and blind spots before every lane change, every time.
3. Planning exits early so you are in the correct lane well before the ramp.
4. Keeping a safe following distance even when other drivers do not.

Our G road test highway tips (/blog/g-road-test-highway-tips/) go through the full checklist examiners look for.

## Where do North York drivers take their road test?

There are several DriveTest centres across Toronto, and North York students book whichever one has a date that suits them. Some of our students choose Metro East in Scarborough, where we teach often. Check the current list of centres and available dates on drivetest.ca (https://drivetest.ca/), since availability changes often.

Whichever centre you pick, it helps to spend your last lesson on the roads around it. Our guide to Metro East DriveTest (/blog/metro-east-drivetest-tips/) covers that centre in detail.

## How many lessons will you need?

Ontario does not set a minimum number of lessons. It does set waiting periods: you must hold your G1 for 12 months before your G2 road test, or 8 months if you finish a government-approved driver education course. After that, you hold your G2 for 12 months before you can take the G road test.

As a rough guide for North York students:

1. Confident drivers who practise often with family usually need 2 to 3 hours of test-focused lessons.
2. Drivers who still hesitate at left turns, lane changes or busy intersections usually need 4 to 5 hours.
3. Complete beginners do best with 10 hours or a full BDE course.

For the signs that you are ready to book, read how many driving lessons you need before your G2 (/blog/how-many-driving-lessons-before-g2/). To see the whole path from G1 to a full licence, our G1 to G timeline (/blog/g1-to-g-licence-timeline-ontario/) lays it out step by step.

## How much do driving lessons cost in North York?

These are Public Star's current prices. HST is 13%, and the total is in brackets.

| Package | Price |
| --- | --- |
| G2 1 hour lesson | $50 + HST ($56.50) |
| G2 3 hours + road test | $250 + HST ($282.50) |
| G2 5 hours + road test | $330 + HST ($372.90) |
| G2 10 hours + road test | $550 + HST ($621.50) |
| G 1 hour lesson | $60 + HST ($67.80) |
| G 3 hours + road test | $300 + HST ($339.00) |
| G 5 hours + road test | $400 + HST ($452.00) |
| BDE Basic | $499 + HST ($563.87) |
| BDE Premium | $649 + HST ($733.37) |
| BDE Advanced | $799 + HST ($902.87) |

Every hours plus road test bundle includes a warm-up before your test and the use of our instructor's car on test day. The road test fee itself is paid to DriveTest and is not included; check the current amount on drivetest.ca (https://drivetest.ca/tests/fees/). For every package, see our driving lesson price guide (/blog/driving-lessons-cost-ontario/).

## Is the BDE course worth it for North York drivers?

A government-approved BDE course lets you take your G2 road test after 8 months instead of 12. Many insurers also offer a discount to new drivers who complete one, so ask your insurance company before you decide. Our BDE packages combine online theory with one-on-one in-car lessons in North York and the surrounding area. Read whether the BDE course is worth it (/blog/is-bde-course-worth-it/) for a fuller comparison.

## Tips for getting the most out of your lessons

- Practise between lessons. Even 20 minutes on quiet streets helps new skills stick.
- Learn to expect the unexpected. Pedestrians, cyclists and buses pulling out are part of every North York drive, so keep scanning.
- Ask questions. Your instructor would rather explain a right of way rule twice than watch you guess on test day.
- Know the common mistakes. Read our list of G2 road test automatic fails (/blog/g2-road-test-automatic-fails/) before you book.

## Do you teach outside North York?

Yes. We are based in Ajax, and our instructors also teach in Scarborough, Pickering, Whitby and Oshawa, with free pick-up and drop-off within our service area. If you live east of North York, our guides to driving lessons in Pickering (/blog/driving-lessons-pickering/) and driving lessons in Ajax (/blog/driving-lessons-ajax/) cover those cities too.

## Frequently asked questions

### Do you offer pick-up in North York?

Yes. Your instructor picks you up from your home, school or workplace in North York and drops you off after the lesson at no extra charge.

### Can I practise on Highway 401 with a G1?

Only with a certified driving instructor. G1 drivers cannot use 400-series highways with a family member, but when you drive with an instructor certified in Ontario, you can drive on any road.

### Which DriveTest centre should I book from North York?

Book whichever Toronto-area centre has a date that works for you, and check drivetest.ca for current openings. Then plan a lesson on the roads around that centre before test day.

### Can I use your car for my road test?

Yes. Every hours plus road test bundle, and the Premium and Advanced BDE packages, include the use of our car on test day along with a warm-up beforehand.

### Can I take lessons without signing up for BDE?

Yes. You can book a single lesson or an hours plus road test bundle as soon as you have your G1.
